01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
heading
A title at the top of a page or section.
reference number
A number used to identify a document.
gap
A missing part in a series.
panel
A group of people who make a decision.
covering sheet
A page placed at the front of a set of documents.
appeal
A request to change or review a decision.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma looked at the three headings in her notebook: Applied, Selected, Paid. The trust had found part of an old list, but Fiona had not sent it. Emma wanted to know more. She did not want to put pressure on Fiona to share private information about students.

The next morning, Fiona called her.

“I can tell you something about the papers,” she said. “The records team has counted the pages we have. The list begins at reference number eleven and ends at number twenty-six. There are gaps between some numbers.”

“Does that mean twenty-six students applied?” Emma asked.

“No. Numbers can be used more than once for different years, and some forms may never have been completed. We cannot use the last number as a total.”

Fiona said she could send a description of the documents, but not the names of students. She was still checking what information could be shared.

“Do you know who made the decisions?” Emma asked.

“The blank form has a space for a panel's decision. I haven't found a complete record of the people on that panel.”

Emma thanked her. She wrote down what Fiona had actually said. She had not seen the pages herself.

Sarah called during lunch.

“We have a list from eleven to twenty-six. That's useful, isn't it?”

“It is a clue. But we don't know how many people applied, who was selected or who was paid.”

Emma went back to the newspaper archive. She searched for another report about the travel scheme. There was a short article published in early October 2011. It said that some students were waiting for information about their travel grants. It did not say which students or whether they had been selected.

This mattered to Emma. Waiting for a reply was not the same as waiting for money. The article did not explain the difference.

She saved a copy and sent Sarah the date and title. They agreed not to publish any conclusion before comparing the original documents.

That evening, Emma received a brief message from Fiona: “One folder contains a covering sheet. Its heading is 'Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011'. I have not checked the contents.”

Emma stared at the words. Someone might have asked the trust to reconsider a decision. Or the sheet might have been prepared for a process that was never used.

She put a question mark beside the heading. This was the first time she had seen a possible way to understand the parent's old complaint. But it was not yet an answer.

She closed her notebook. Tomorrow, she would ask what the trust meant by an appeal.
